q: London (dispersion) forces between molecules arise from:
o: Hydrogen atoms bonded to N, O or F
Temporary dipoles that form in one molecule and induce dipoles in its neighbours
Transfer of electrons from one molecule to another
x: Electron clouds shift for an instant, giving a temporary dipole that induces another in a neighbouring molecule; these forces exist between all molecules, even non-polar ones. Permanent dipoles give dipole–dipole forces instead.

q: Which compound cannot form hydrogen bonds between its own molecules, but can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules?
x: Propanone has no H on O or N, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, but the lone pairs on its C=O oxygen accept hydrogen bonds from water. Methanol and ammonia hydrogen-bond with themselves; methane can do neither.

q: Which order of boiling points is correct?
x: All three hydrogen-bond. Water forms two hydrogen bonds per molecule (two H and two lone pairs), building a 3D network, so it boils highest (100 °C); HF boils at about 20 °C and NH₃ at about −33 °C. Ranking by electronegativity alone puts HF on top.

q: Molecules of which compound attract each other by dipole–dipole forces?
x: CHCl₃ is tetrahedral but unsymmetrical, so its bond dipoles do not cancel and it is polar. CCl₄ (tetrahedral), CO₂ (linear) and BF₃ (trigonal planar) have polar bonds whose dipoles cancel, so the molecules are non-polar.

q: Propane (CH₃CH₂CH₃, 44 g mol⁻¹), methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃, 46 g mol⁻¹) and ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH, 46 g mol⁻¹) have similar molar masses. Their boiling points increase in the order:
x: With similar London forces, the extra forces decide: propane is non-polar (London only), methoxymethane is polar (dipole–dipole) but has no O–H, and ethanol has O–H groups that hydrogen-bond. Treating the ether as hydrogen-bonded puts it above ethanol.

q: Ice floats on liquid water because:
o: Ice molecules have less mass than liquid water molecules
Covalent bonds in ice are longer than in liquid water
Hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules in ice in an open cage-like structure with empty spaces
There are no hydrogen bonds in ice
x: In ice each molecule is hydrogen-bonded to four others in a fixed open (tetrahedral) arrangement, so ice takes up more volume than the same mass of liquid and is less dense. When ice melts some hydrogen bonds break and the molecules pack closer.

q: When the temperature of a liquid is raised, its surface tension:
x: Faster-moving molecules weaken the effect of intermolecular attractions at the surface, so surface tension falls as temperature rises (as viscosity does).

q: Glycerol, CH₂(OH)CH(OH)CH₂OH, is much more viscous than water. The main reason is that:
o: Each glycerol molecule has three O–H groups and forms many hydrogen bonds with its neighbours
Glycerol molecules move faster than water molecules
x: Three O–H groups per molecule give an extensive hydrogen-bonded network, and the larger molecules also have stronger London forces, so layers resist flowing past each other.

q: Evaporation of a liquid causes cooling because:
o: The molecules left behind gain energy from the escaping ones
Evaporation happens only at the boiling point
Vapour molecules absorb heat from the air
The molecules with the highest kinetic energy escape, so the average kinetic energy of those left falls
x: Only molecules with enough energy to overcome the attractions leave the surface; removing the fastest ones lowers the average kinetic energy, and so the temperature, of the remaining liquid. Evaporation happens at all temperatures, not only at the boiling point.

q: Two closed flasks at 25 °C contain water: one holds 10 cm³ with a small surface, the other 100 cm³ with a much larger surface. Once equilibrium is reached, the vapour pressure of water is:
o: Greater in the flask with more water
Greater in the flask with the larger surface
Greater in the flask with less water
x: Equilibrium vapour pressure depends only on the liquid and its temperature. A larger surface makes evaporation and condensation both faster, so equilibrium is reached sooner but at the same pressure.

q: How much heat is needed to change 18 g of ice at 0 °C into steam at 100 °C? (Enthalpy of fusion of ice = 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy of vaporisation of water = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹; specific heat of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; H = 1, O = 16)
x: 18 g is 1 mol. Melting: 6.0 kJ. Heating water 0 → 100 °C: 18 × 4.2 × 100 = 7560 J = 7.56 kJ. Boiling: 40.7 kJ. Total = 54.26 ≈ 54.3 kJ. Leaving out the heating step gives 46.7 kJ, and leaving out melting gives 48.3 kJ.

q: Ice is an example of a:
x: Ice is made of separate H₂O molecules held in the lattice by hydrogen bonds, so it is a molecular solid. The covalent O–H bonds are only inside each molecule, not a continuous network as in diamond.

q: Diamond is extremely hard and has a very high melting point because:
o: Its carbon atoms are held by London forces only
It contains free electrons that bind the atoms
Its carbon atoms are held by ionic bonds
Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a continuous three-dimensional network
x: In diamond each sp³ carbon is joined tetrahedrally to four others, so melting or scratching it means breaking many strong covalent bonds. Free delocalised electrons belong to graphite and metals.

q: Ionic crystals such as NaCl are brittle and shatter when struck. This is because when one layer of ions is pushed over another:
o: The electrons in the crystal move freely and hold the layers together
The covalent bonds between the ions break
The ions turn into neutral atoms
Ions of like charge come face to face and repel, so the crystal splits
x: A small shift brings Na⁺ next to Na⁺ and Cl⁻ next to Cl⁻, and the strong repulsion splits the crystal. In metals the delocalised electrons keep the layers bonded after a shift, which is why metals bend instead.

q: Iodine crystals are soft and sublime easily on gentle warming, although the I–I bond inside each molecule is a strong covalent bond. This is because:
o: Iodine forms a covalent network like diamond
The I₂ molecules in the crystal are held together only by weak London forces
The I–I bonds break on gentle warming
x: Iodine is a molecular solid: subliming it separates whole I₂ molecules by overcoming weak London forces, and the covalent I–I bonds stay intact. Confusing breaking intermolecular forces with breaking bonds is the usual slip.

q: Arrange ice, sodium, sodium chloride and quartz (SiO₂) in order of increasing melting point.
x: Ice (molecular, hydrogen bonds) melts at 0 °C; sodium (weak metallic bonding, one electron per atom) at about 98 °C; NaCl (ionic) at about 801 °C; quartz (covalent network) above 1600 °C. Assuming every metal melts higher than an ionic solid puts sodium above NaCl.

q: All crystals can be grouped into how many crystal systems?
x: There are seven crystal systems: cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal and rhombohedral (trigonal). 14 is the number of Bravais lattices and 6 is the number of unit-cell parameters.

q: A metal crystallises in a body-centred cubic unit cell, with an atom at each corner and one at the centre of the cube. The number of atoms belonging to one unit cell is:
x: Each corner atom is shared by 8 cells: 8 × ⅛ = 1, plus 1 whole atom at the centre = 2. Counting all nine atoms as whole gives 9; 4 is the count for a face-centred cubic cell.

q: The lattice energy of MgO is about four times that of NaF, although the ions in the two crystals are of similar size. The main reason is that:
o: The charges on both ions are doubled (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻), and attraction depends on the product of the charges
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are much larger than Na⁺ and F⁻
MgO is a covalent network solid
MgO has a higher molar mass than NaF
x: Lattice energy grows with the product of the ion charges and falls with the distance between them. With similar ionic radii, 2 × 2 = 4 compared with 1 × 1 = 1 gives about four times the lattice energy. Larger ions would lower it, not raise it.

q: In a cubic unit cell, atoms of P occupy all the corners and atoms of Q occupy the centres of all the faces. The simplest formula of the compound is:
x: Corners: 8 × ⅛ = 1 P. Face centres: 6 × ½ = 3 Q. So the formula is PQ₃. Counting each face atom as a whole (6 Q to 1 P) gives PQ₆.

q: A unit cell has a = b ≠ c and α = β = γ = 90°. It belongs to the:
x: Two equal edges with all angles 90° is tetragonal. Cubic needs all three edges equal, orthorhombic has all three different, and hexagonal has one angle of 120°.
